blocks.title: Words To Keep Straight
blocks.text: The value is the referent, the act is a borrow, and the window in which the reference must stay valid is its lifetime. A `&String` points at the stack triple, not at the heap bytes.

items: `&T` grants read access, never mutation through it.
Many `&T` to one value may coexist — aliasing is fine.
No mutation means no reader ever sees a torn value.
Mutating the owner while a `&T` is live is E0502.

items: `&T` is itself `Copy`: assigning duplicates the pointer.
Pass a `&T` to ten functions, still hold it after.
Method calls auto-borrow: `v.len()` is `Vec::len(&v)`.
Never write `&v` by hand for a method receiver.

blocks.title: Widest Callers Win
blocks.text: A `fn f(s: &str)` accepts `&String`, `&str` and string literals. A `fn f(s: &String)` accepts only one of the three for no benefit.

items: Returning `&T` ties the result's lifetime to the receiver.
`v.first()` keeps `v` borrowed for as long as you hold it.
`for x in &v` yields `&T` and leaves `v` owned after.
`for x in v` moves `v` into the loop and consumes it.
`&T` for a sized `T` is exactly one machine word.
`&str` and `&[T]` are fat pointers: pointer plus length.
`&&T` appears in closures: `filter(|x: &&i32| **x > 0)`.
Auto-deref hides the double reference in comparisons.

blocks.title: Threads Read For Free
items: `&T` is `Send` exactly when `T: Sync`.
That is the basis of scoped-thread read sharing.
No lock needed while nobody can write.

blocks.q: Why does pushing inside a `&self` method fail?
a_bullets: `&self` is a shared borrow of the whole struct.
`push` needs exclusive access to the field.
example_code: fn add(&self, x: i32) { self.items.push(x); } // no
fn add(&mut self, x: i32) { self.items.push(x); }

blocks.title: Start Here Every Time
blocks.text: Default every parameter to `&T`. Escalate to `&mut T` only when you must write, and to owned `T` only when you must store or consume.

items: `&mut T` grants write access and excludes all others.
No other reference, shared or mutable, may coexist.
The core rule: one `&mut T`, or any number of `&T`.
Never both at the same program point.
The owner must be mutable: `let mut v = ...;` first.
Borrowing `&mut v` from a non-`mut` binding is E0596.
`&mut T` is not `Copy` — passing it moves it.
Unless the compiler reborrows for you, which it usually does.

blocks.text: A `&mut Vec<&'long str>` is not usable as `&mut Vec<&'short str>`. If it were, a caller could push short-lived data into long-lived storage and read it after the data died.

blocks.title: Signatures Are The Contract
blocks.text: A method returning `&T` borrows the whole receiver even if its body never touches most of it. The checker never reads the body — inline the field access when that bites.

blocks.title: Annotations Change Nothing
blocks.text: Writing `'a` does not make data live longer. It only tells the compiler which input a reference points into, so it can check the region you already have.

blocks.title: 'static Is Not Immortal
blocks.text: `T: 'static` is a bound on what `T` may contain, not a promise the value lives forever. An owned `String` satisfies `T: 'static` and still drops at the end of its scope.

blocks.title: Two Things Named Alike
blocks.text: The lifetime of a reference variable is its scope. The lifetime parameter on a type constrains the referent's region. Lifetimes are erased before codegen: zero representation, zero cost.

It is declared in the angle brackets like a type parameter.
Without it the compiler cannot tell which input you return.

blocks.text: Never add a lifetime to make an error go away. First answer: which data does this output actually point into? The annotation then writes itself, or you learn the answer is "nothing" and you should return owned.

blocks.text: The checker cannot prove two index ranges are disjoint, so the standard library proves it by hand and hands you a safe signature. That is the pattern: unsafe inside, sound API outside.
